witchel:micro:2001: The citing literature engages the design chiefly in discussion rather than construction. Papers on way-halting caches, speculative way caching, and heterogeneous way-size caches describe the tag-unchecked access scheme in detail when setting out hardware-only routes to the same energy savings, and compiler-enabled approaches — Xtream-fit, and work coupling compiler-enabled with conventional memory accessing — measure against it. Most other citations are brief placements in the energy-efficient cache literature. The idea also resurfaces in another register: Ceviche adopts direct addressing in a capability-enhanced design for secure virtualization of caches.
kjolstad:tog:2016: Outside the project, citing works engage Simit chiefly as a design point in the space of domain-specific languages. Tensor Comprehensions and Taichi position their abstractions against Simit's dual graph-and-matrix view, SymX measures its symbolic-expression simulator against Simit as a baseline, and papers across graphics and compiler venues list it as an example of a language built for physical simulation. Much of the remainder is passing mention in work on simulation and sparse linear algebra, so the deep external engagement is thin: Simit appears more often as the system others define themselves relative to than as one they extend. The language and compiler are available at simit-lang/simit.
VarStudy2023: In the lattice-QCD literature the study's reception centers on its cautionary result. Papers on multi-baryon spectroscopy cite the interpolating-operator dependence as a systematic concern in interpreting two-nucleon spectra, and a follow-up by Detmold and collaborators extends the analysis with further constraints on the finite-volume spectrum at the same pion mass. The computed spectra serve as input elsewhere: a constraint of pionless effective field theory uses them directly, and calculations of neutrinoless double-beta decay in finite volume take them as benchmarks, while the sparsened-propagator machinery reappears in nucleon-pion spectroscopy. The other citations are brief mentions in the two-nucleon discussion and in reviews of the field.
maydan:lcpc:1992: The citation record reflects that supersession: the workshop version is cited sparsely, and mostly in passing. The most visible thread is the runtime-parallelization line of Rauchwerger and Padua, whose LRPD-test papers list it among the compile-time analyses their speculative approach sidesteps; surveys of automatic parallelization place it alongside its contemporaries, and occasional works cite its treatment of array data-flow as supporting evidence. One later effort on accurate array data-flow analysis engages the mathematics directly. A fair share of the record is unjudged, but what has been examined suggests a paper read chiefly through its POPL successor.
taylor:isscc:2003: To the circuits community the paper is the Raw chip's entry in the record of multicore silicon, cited chiefly as an exemplar: networks-on-chip and multiprocessor system-on-chip surveys list the design when cataloguing tiled interconnects, and low-power on-chip network work differentiates its choices from Raw's. The more engaged citations measure against the chip — AsAP reports comparisons with it, a performance analysis of PIM, stream, and tiled processing exercised it on memory-intensive signal-processing kernels, and knowledge-based STAP algorithm work used it as a platform — while the TILE64 paper discusses the design at length. The record is modest and mostly peripheral, consistent with an implementation paper whose ideas circulate through its companions.
zhao:cc:2008: The wider citing literature treats EDDI mainly as a reference point: it appears in related-work sections of debugging, instrumentation, and tracing papers as the demonstration that software watchpoints can scale far beyond the hardware debug registers. A handful of works engage more directly — lightweight memory tracing differentiates its design from EDDI's, and PinADX discusses it in detail — but no external system in the record builds on the tool itself. What circulates is the result: papers from time-travel debugging to undefined-value detection cite the million-watchpoint figure as the reference point for instrumentation-based monitoring at scale.
ansel:cases:2012: The external citation record is thin and plain about it: no citing system adopts the racing design, and most references are brief mentions in the online-autotuning and adaptive-systems literature. Where the paper is discussed at length it is as a design point; Wang and O'Boyle's account of machine learning in compiler optimization describes the approach, and mARGOt situates its own dynamic autotuning framework relative to it. The most consistent audience is the self-aware and energy-aware systems line around Hoffmann, where JouleGuard, CoAdapt, and MEANTIME cite it among prior adaptive systems. In that literature SiblingRivalry figures as an example of always-on adaptation, cited for the idea more than built upon.
amin:iccd:2009: The reception sits almost entirely in the microfluidic design-automation literature that formed around flow-based chips in the following decade. Control-layer synthesis work — control synthesis for flow-based microfluidic large-scale integration biochips, control-layer routing and control-pin minimization, integrated flow-control codesign — treats the paper's control-line minimization and valve-routing algorithms as an early formulation to refine or generalize, and its discussions of the paper are often detailed rather than perfunctory. Micado itself found users: Fluigi builds on it, and work on automatic synthesis of microfluidic chips from a domain-specific language employs it. The remaining citations place the paper among the origins of CAD for mVLSI biochips.
bruening:fddo:2001: Among the examined citations the reception is that of infrastructure: many come from work that ran the framework rather than merely mentioning it. Vigilante and the foreign-code detection work on the Windows/x86 platform built on it; Smith and Hazelwood's study of code cache management and later measurements of dynamic binary translators' hardware-cache impact took it as a subject system; work on indirect branch emulation in virtual machines drew on it as tooling. Duesterwald's account of the design and engineering of a dynamic binary optimizer revisits the same ground from the Dynamo side. Many citing works are unjudged, so the picture is partial, but among the judged, users outnumber mentioners — unusual for a workshop paper. The framework lives on as DynamoRIO/dynamorio on GitHub.
sullivan:ivme:2003: Outside the project the technique found few direct users, LIFT applying the same instrumentation substrate to information-flow tracking for security, and the record is otherwise mostly peripheral: the paper appears in passing wherever interpreter overhead or trace formation is discussed, and the survey of adaptive optimization in virtual machines fixes its place among the era's approaches. The closer engagements come from the interpreter-implementation literature: context threading cites its findings, YETI positions its own design against it, and Tracing the meta-level gives it one of its more detailed readings. The approach stands in the literature as an early attempt to make trace-based optimization see through an interpreter to the program it runs. The DynamoRIO framework on which the work is built lives on in the DynamoRIO/dynamorio repository.
lamb:pldi:2003: External reception is quieter than the project's internal use: a sizable share of the citing record is StreamIt's own papers and theses, and most outside citations name the work in passing when listing the compiler's optimizations. The clearest line of uptake runs through sketching — Solar-Lezama's StreamBit takes the linear framework as its point of departure, and programming by sketching for bit-streaming programs carries that agenda forward — while the static-analysis community, in Feret's analysis of digital filters and Monniaux's compositional analysis of floating-point linear filters, cites it when treating linear filters as objects of formal study; Sigma* sets its own approach apart from this compile-time analysis. The compiler and its optimizations live on in the bthies/streamit repository.
lee:micro:2002: Reception outside that toolchain is compact but concrete. The most sustained take-up is a transplant: Baraglia, Capannini, and colleagues carried the confidence-weighted, multi-pass design into job scheduling for large computing farms, first adopting the idea and then extending it into a multi-criteria framework, while Win and Wong applied the cooperative-pass approach to instruction scheduling with linear-scan register allocation. Within spatial-architecture compilation the paper is mostly a point of reference: the EDGE static-placement work measures against it, and modulo-scheduling papers for coarse-grained reconfigurable architectures position their schedulers relative to it. The remainder cites it in passing among spatial scheduling techniques.
zhang:dascmp:2007: Reception of the layer itself is modest and concentrated in the stream-compilation community. The substantive engagement came from Flextream, which used the framework in adaptive compilation of streaming applications for heterogeneous architectures, and from Streamware, which positions its own approach against it. Most other citations are brief: work on executing stream programs on GPUs, accelerators, and multiprocessor systems names the paper among StreamIt-based multicore backends when recounting how stream programs have been mapped to parallel hardware. The record is that of one system in a cluster of Cell-era streaming runtimes, cited together as a generation. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure, in which the Cell backend was built, lives on in the bthies/streamit repository.
zhao:cgo:2010: External users followed the same pattern, building tools on Umbra rather than writing about it: comprehensive kernel instrumentation via dynamic binary translation, the MINIME benchmark synthesizer, the Taint Rabbit's optimized taint analysis, and machine-learned detection of parallel patterns all employ its shadow-memory framework. Neighboring designs engage it as a reference point — the case for unlimited watchpoints measures against it, and AddressSanitizer positions its own shadow scheme relative to Umbra's translation. The rest of the record is brief: dynamic-analysis papers list Umbra among memory-shadowing systems. The citations are not many, but the most substantive of them come from people who used the framework.
thies:ppopp:2005: Reception of the construct divides between the project's orbit and the dataflow community. Within StreamIt, teleport messaging is exercised by application studies — stream programming for image and video compression, image-based motion estimation — and a sizable share of the citing record is the project's own. Outside it, the closest engagement comes from Edward A. Lee's group: Bui, Patel, and Lee adopt the sdep formalism to check circular dependencies in distributed stream programs, and Bui's dissertation on scheduling stream programs extends it. Elsewhere the paper is described more than used — SoC-C differentiates its own treatment of control in embedded software, and many citations recount the mechanism in detail without building on it. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure lives on at bthies/streamit.
zhao:vee:2011: The reception centers on the false sharing detectors that followed. SHERIFF, PREDATOR, and Cheetah position their designs against its instrumentation-based approach, ScaAnalyzer differentiates its scalability analysis from it, and the DARWIN framework adopted its ideas for detecting false sharing in OpenMP applications. A second strand cites the paper as evidence — that false sharing degrades performance on multicore machines, or that dynamic binary instrumentation can expose it — while the remaining citations are passing mentions in work on contention, scheduling, and performance analysis. The engaged readership is small and concentrated among builders of sharing detectors, for whom the tool is the design each successor explains itself against.
thies:pldi:2001: Within the polyhedral compilation literature the framework became part of the standard background: works on automatic parallelization, AlphaZ, and the Sparse Polyhedral Framework cite it in passing when surveying affine scheduling and memory optimization. The engaged reception is narrower and mathematical. Darte and Schreiber's lattice-based memory allocation examines the occupancy-vector formulation in detail, and Touati and Eisenbeis carried the joint schedule–storage view into periodic register allocation on ILP processors, with later work adopting the formulation for periodic task scheduling with storage minimization; a study of LLM-guided loop optimization returned to its examples as benchmarks. The citations are not numerous, but those that engage do so with the mathematics.
gottschlich:mapl:2018: The vocabulary is what circulated. Citing papers rarely engage the taxonomy in depth; instead they invoke it to locate their own work within machine programming, and they come from the breadth the paper called for — learned database systems such as Bao and RadixSpline, neural-network verification, program synthesis, even the inference of chemical procedures from text. Nearly all of these citations are peripheral: the paper is cited for its framing, as position papers are, its three-pillar scheme serving as shorthand for a research agenda rather than as a technique anyone extends.
og-cgo20: Among external citers the paper serves mainly as a point of comparison: the evaluation of graph frameworks on the GAP Benchmark Suite, work on efficient stepping algorithms for parallel shortest paths, and a scalable architecture for reprioritizing ordered parallelism all measure against the ordered GraphIt implementations, and Cache-Efficient Fork-Processing Patterns on Large Graphs draws on its findings. The larger remainder is list membership, with hardware accelerators and concurrent graph systems such as GraphPulse and Glign citing it among the compilers and frameworks for ordered graph processing. The engaged citations are comparative rather than constructive — outside the group's own successors, the paper is measured against more often than built on. The implementation lives in the GraphIt-DSL/graphit repository, and a badged artifact with availability, functionality, and reproduction badges accompanies the paper on Zenodo.
larsen:pact:2002: External reception settled in the short-vector compilation community, for which alignment was a shared obstacle. Eichenberger, Wu, and O'Brien's vectorization for SIMD architectures with alignment constraints engages the paper in detail, the CELL processor compiler cites it as evidence, and work on runtime alignment and length conversion, on multi-platform auto-vectorization, and on SIMD compilation for embedded processors positions its own alignment handling relative to it. The idea traveled outside compilers as well: T4 adopted the congruence idea in compiling sequential code for speculative parallelization in hardware. The citations are not numerous and many are brief, but the detailed engagements come from groups whose own work centered on alignment analysis.
senanayake2020sparse: The uptake runs deepest inside the sparse-compilation community. Mosaic builds its interoperable tensor-algebra compiler on the framework, Stardust extends it toward reconfigurable dataflow hardware, the compilation of modular and general sparse workspaces continues the workspaces line, and the Sparse Abstract Machine, DISTAL, and a compiler for fused relational operations on multisets carry its ideas elsewhere. Others use it as a measuring stick: polyhedral code generation for sparse contraction and register tiling for unstructured sparsity compare against it, and BaCO tunes over its scheduling space. The remaining citations mostly place the paper in lists of sparse tensor compilers, so the record is compact but substantive at its center. The implementation is available in the tensor-compiler/taco repository at the oopsla2020 branch.
kjolstad:2018:workspaces: Among the paper's citers the sparse-compilation community predominates, and its engagement is unusually direct: a large fraction of the citing works extend or build on the transformation rather than merely mention it. MLIR's sparse tensor support adopts the workspace idea, and a line of TACO-descended systems — Mosaic, SparseLNR, and compilers for sparse tensor convolutions and shape operators — extends the mechanism itself, with later work on modular and general sparse workspaces generalizing the dense scratch arrays to sparse ones. Hardware-oriented compilers such as the Sparse Abstract Machine, Stardust, CoNST, and FuseFlow build on the generated kernels and the scheduling vocabulary. The record is small but dense with successors, and the implementation lives on in the tensor-compiler/taco repository.
hall:lcpc:1995: External engagement clusters around the SUIF system itself: the studies measuring and evaluating automatic parallelization in SUIF run the framework, SUIF Explorer builds interactive parallelization on top of it, and the case for combining compile-time and run-time parallelization extends the analyses. Farther out, the paper appears in surveys and reference works on parallel computing and in passing citations crediting interprocedural analysis as an ingredient of automatic parallelization. The record is small, and close to half of the external citations are unjudged, so the visible reception is chiefly the SUIF community building on its own foundation.
hall:toplas:2005: As the archival form of work whose earlier versions had already circulated, the article draws a modest citation record, most of it brief: papers cite it as the reference for SUIF's interprocedural parallelization or as evidence of what automatic parallelization achieved on scientific codes. The closest engagement comes from lines that continued the analyses — Hall's own work on predicated array data-flow analysis measures against it, her code isolator and empirical sparse-solver study draw on it, and Rus and Rauchwerger's work on migrating sequential code to multi-threaded architectures takes it as a baseline. Farther afield the citations thin to passing mentions in later parallelization work, from behavior-oriented parallelization to Futhark.
karczmarek:lctes:2003: Outside the group the citation record is modest and stays close to stream compilation. The most engaged use is in mobile sensing, where work on static memory management builds on the schedules and a follow-on line adopts the ideas; the buffer-space efficient, deadlock-free scheduling work of Park and Dally cites its results as evidence about the code-size and buffer-space tradeoff. Evaluations of other stream systems reuse its benchmarks, and most remaining citations are brief mentions situating new schedulers against StreamIt. It is a paper cited within one community — mostly as background, occasionally as a foundation. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure lives on at bthies/streamit.
